definition: In artificial intelligence and related fields, an argumentation framework is a way to deal with contentious information and draw conclusions from it using formalized arguments.
details: In an abstract argumentation framework, entry-level information is a set of abstract arguments that, for instance, represent data or a proposition. Conflicts between arguments are represented by a binary relation on the set of arguments. In concrete terms, an argumentation framework is represented with a directed graph such that the nodes are the arguments, and the arrows represent the attack relation. There exist some extensions of the Dung's framework, like the logic-based argumentation frameworks or the value-based argumentation frameworks.

explainer.lead: An argumentation framework turns a disagreement into a structured set of arguments and attacks between them. This gives AI systems a formal way to represent contentious information and work toward conclusions without treating every claim as uncontested fact.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a class debate where each idea is written on a card, and an arrow means one card challenges another. Laying out the cards and arrows helps everyone see the disagreement clearly. An argumentation framework does this formally so a computer can reason from arguments that conflict.
tiers.practitioner: Represent arguments as nodes and attacks as directed edges, keeping abstract argument identifiers separate from any data or propositions they represent. The graph captures conflict structure, but the abstract model does not itself explain how arguments were constructed or whether an attack is justified. Logic-based and value-based frameworks are available when Dung's abstract representation needs extending.
tiers.paperLevel: An abstract argumentation framework can be written AF = (A, R), where A is a set of abstract arguments and R ⊆ A × A is a binary attack relation. Thus (a, b) ∈ R means that argument a attacks argument b, making the framework a directed graph. Dung's framework has extensions including logic-based and value-based argumentation frameworks; its abstract form does not encode arguments' internal structure or the grounds for attacks.

explainer.example: Let A be “The pavement is wet, so it rained,” and B be “A cleaner just washed the pavement, so its wetness is not evidence of rain.” Add C: “The cleaner was not working today,” which challenges B. The graph is C → B → A, with both arrows representing attacks.

usedIn.name: Artificial intelligence
usedIn.detail: Represents contentious information and conflicting arguments as a basis for drawing formal conclusions.

usedIn.name: Formal argumentation
usedIn.detail: Uses Dung's abstract framework as the basis for variants such as logic-based and value-based argumentation frameworks.

explainer.intuition: Instead of flattening a dispute into isolated facts, keep the competing arguments and record which ones challenge which. The result is a map of conflict that can support formal conclusion-drawing.
howItWorks: Start with a set of abstract arguments, which may represent data or propositions.
Define a binary attack relation over those arguments.
Draw each argument as a node in a directed graph.
Draw an arrow from one argument to another when the first attacks the second.
Use the resulting framework to reason about conclusions from the contentious information.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a precise, compact way to handle conflict rather than ignoring it or prematurely choosing one claim. The same graph representation also connects abstract reasoning to richer logic-based and value-based approaches.
misconceptions: An arrow represents an attack, not support or agreement.
An abstract argument need not contain explicit logical reasoning; it can stand for data or a proposition.
The graph records arguments and attacks, but does not by itself explain why an attack is justified.
